summary:
Visitors to Indiana stand under the United States national framework on travel documents and entry. Executive Order 14168 of January 2025 requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department stopped processing the X marker and now issues passports only as M or F from supporting documents, while passports already issued with an X remain valid until expiry. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, the ACLU is suing the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and in November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed the department to proceed with its changed treatment. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking entry to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas, with applicants flagged under the code 'SWS25'.

Within Indiana, the route to a corrected gender marker on a driver's licence or state identification card closed on 1 February 2026, when the Bureau of Motor Vehicles ban took effect. The change ended what had been a long-standing path through a court-ordered gender change or a physician statement, and it culminated an administrative rule change the Bureau initiated. LGBTQ advocates who testified against it warned that it will forcibly out transgender and nonbinary residents whenever their documents are inspected.

Birth-certificate markers were already closed to amendment before that rule. In May 2023 the Indiana Supreme Court declined, in split votes, to hear two cases brought by transgender girls seeking to change the sex designation on their birth certificates, leaving in place appeals-court rulings that trial courts lack authority to grant such changes unless the Indiana General Assembly codifies them. One of the cases concerned a nine-year-old transgender girl whose birth certificate's male designation allowed her school to restrict her bathroom access.

The Indiana Senate approved Senate Bill 182 by a 37-8 party-line vote on 27 January 2026 and sent it to the House. The bill would require public K-12 schools and state universities to designate multi-person restrooms, locker rooms and changing areas for use only by males or females based on reproductive biology at birth, barring transgender students from facilities matching their gender identity. It would also create statutory definitions for sex and gender, bar amendments to birth certificates, and restrict housing in prisons. Author Sen. Liz Brown, R-Fort Wayne, said the proposal lets women continue to have private spaces; GenderNexus and other opponents argued that allowing anyone 'directly or indirectly injured' to sue a school over an alleged violation would invite harassment-style enforcement.

A February 2026 national anti-trans legal risk assessment places Indiana among the harshest anti-trans states in the country, citing the 2026 identity-document policy and the escalation of bathroom restrictions as the drivers of adult risk.
tangentialFactors:
Indiana sits within a wider national pattern rather than apart from it. A Movement Advancement Project tally counts state bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings in nine states and one territory, with outright state bans on facility use per gender identity in additional states; 29 states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban. Indiana's Senate Bill 182 would move the state toward the restricted column on both schools and, through its housing provision, correctional facilities.

Indiana's birth-certificate position resembles that of other states where court rulings have closed the door pending legislation. Kansas enacted a law in February 2026 preventing transgender people from changing markers on birth certificates and driver's licences and invalidating existing documents that do not match sex assigned at birth; rights groups described that statute as a template for other states, and Indiana's pending bill follows a comparable structure.

The February 2026 assessment that ranks Indiana among the harshest states is one of several national instruments tracking trans risk, alongside a July 2026 national risk assessment that flagged Idaho as the fourth state to receive a 'Do Not Travel' designation for trans people. Indiana does not carry that designation in the sources available here.

Facility arrests elsewhere show what enforcement of such provisions can produce: in April 2025 a transgender student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol, which civil-rights attorneys described as the first known arrest under that state's bathroom-restriction law. No comparable Indiana arrest appears in the sources available here.
localsOnly:
Indiana residents lost the ability to change their gender marker on driver's licences and other state identification cards when the Bureau of Motor Vehicles ban took effect on 1 February 2026. Before that date a court-ordered gender change or a physician statement was sufficient; the administrative rule change initiated by the Bureau removed both. Residents holding older documents issued with a corrected marker are not addressed by the sources available here.

Birth certificates remain unchangeable in practice. The May 2023 Indiana Supreme Court denials left standing appeals-court rulings that trial courts have no authority to grant a birth-certificate sex-designation change unless the General Assembly legislates it, and Senate Bill 182 would put that prohibition into statute.

Senate Bill 182 is not yet law as of the sources available here. It cleared the Senate on 27 January 2026 and awaits House action; its school-facility, birth-certificate, sex-definition and prison-housing provisions would take effect only if it passes the House and is signed. Advocacy groups including GenderNexus testified against it, and LGBTQ advocates who testified on the Bureau of Motor Vehicles rule change warned of forcible outing.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Senate Bill 182 has passed the Indiana House or been signed into law is unresolved in the sources available here; the latest sourced action is the 27 January 2026 Senate vote.

The scope of the Bureau of Motor Vehicles ban is not fully specified: the sources do not state whether it reaches identity cards already issued with a corrected marker, or how the change is applied to Indiana residents whose federal passport still carries an X marker.

Indiana-specific hate-crime coverage, employment and housing protections for gender identity, and any state-level restrictions on gender-affirming care are not sourced in this inventory. The parent framework's federal care measures, including Executive Order 14187 and the October 2025 Medicaid proposed rules, are noted at national level but their application to Indiana visitors and residents is unresolved here.

Enforcement data for Indiana bathroom provisions is unavailable, including any arrests, school discipline cases or private civil suits brought under existing facilities rules in the state.
